title: Hundred-hertz quantum circuit iteration rate in a reusable neutral-atom array
authors: Liang Chen, Wen-Yi Zhu, Dong-Qi Ma, Tian-Yang Zhang, Zi-Jie Chen, Yi-Chen Zhang, Hong-Jie Fan, Guang-Jie Chen, Qing-Xuan Jie, Wei-Zhou Cai, Tian-Cai Zhang, Luyan Sun, Yan-Lei Zhang, Xi-Feng Ren, Guang-Can Guo, Zhu-Bo Wang, Ya-Dong Hu, Gang Li, Chang-Ling Zou
abstract: Neutral-atom quantum processors have rapidly advanced in scale and coherence, yet their practical performance remains constrained by limited quantum circuit iteration rates (qCIRs) and information throughput. Here we experimentally demonstrate a high-throughput neutral-atom system based on non-destructive readout and atom reuse. By integrating a chip-based photonic interface with a 10-qubit array, we implement non-destructive readout with a retention probability of 99.7%, and further achieve a raw qCIR of 101Hz and a post-selected qCIR of 74.8Hz. More importantly, we verify a general throughput optimization methodology and obtain a normalized Fisher information rate of 57.7Hz, improving the achievable throughput by more than one order of magnitude compared with conventional methods. Our results establish a practical route toward high-throughput neutral-atom quantum processors.
summary: This paper reports an experimental demonstration achieving high-throughput operation in a neutral-atom quantum processor by implementing non-destructive readout and atom reuse techniques. By integrating a photonic chip interface, the authors surpassed previous limitations to achieve a post-selected circuit iteration rate of 74.8 Hz. This work establishes a practical pathway toward building scalable, fast quantum computing hardware.
main_problem: The practical performance of neutral-atom quantum processors is limited by low quantum circuit iteration rates (qCIRs) and overall information throughput.
main_result: The authors achieved a post-selected qCIR of 74.8 Hz, significantly improving throughput via an optimized methodology that utilized non-destructive readout and atom reuse.
method: They implemented a high-throughput system using a chip-based photonic interface to enable fast, state-resolved, non-destructive readout and designed a benchmark sequence incorporating atom reuse between circuits.
model_or_system: The platform is a neutral-atom array (using ${}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms) integrated with an optical channel mapping (OCM) chip for parallel site-resolved readout. The core innovation lies in the ability to rapidly cycle qubits without full reloading.
key_observables: Raw qCIR (101 Hz), post-selected qCIR (74.8 Hz), and normalized Fisher information rate (57.7 Hz).
important_parameters: Retention probability of 99.7%; the cycle time is dominated by a $7	ext{ms}$ benchmark cycle.
main_assumptions: The improvement relies on establishing a direct qubit-to-detector correspondence via the OCM chip, enabling non-destructive and fast readout.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup using the photonic chip (Fig. 1), detail the atom reuse benchmark sequence (Fig. 2), and show trade-offs between fidelity/retention probability versus readout duration (Fig. 2(d)).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the throughput bottleneck, then detailing the OCM chip integration for non-destructive readout, demonstrating the atom reuse protocol to achieve high raw qCIRs, and finally optimizing performance using the Fisher information rate.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering hurdle in quantum computing—the speed of operations. The focus on throughput optimization via resource management (atom reuse) is highly relevant for scaling up any physical qubit modality.

Global π-polarized microwave (MW), π-polarized optical-pumping, and σ+-polarized readout fields are used for qubit state initialization, gate operation, and readout.
